Section I. History and Tradition.—In 1588, the Districts of Tipperal: and Noacolly were included in the Sirkar of Sonergaon, one of the nineteen divisions made by the Mogul Administrator, Todur Mull. Sonergaon which at that time included a small portion of Dacca contained fifty-two Perguanahs, and the

snount of its revenue amounted to Rupees 2,58,283. The revenue assessment appcars to have been made on a Mouzawaree, that is, the amount of revenue of cach village was duly specified, an arrangement which reflects great credit on the adiministrative Officers of those days, inasmuch as it affords an excellent basis for the assessinent of the public revenue, and, if strictly adhered to, prevents all fraudulent divisions of estates. Wustory of Administration In 1722, the original Sirkars of Todur Mull, together with those subsequently annexed by Sooltan Shoojah in 1658, were formed into thirteen Chucklahs, or military jurisdictions. one of which, that ot Jehangeernugger (Dacca), included both Tipperah and Noacolly. This extensive circle was sub-divided into a number of Zemindarees, which were classed under the principal one of Jellalpoor. It contained two hundred and thirty-six Pergunnahs, and was assessed at Rupces 19,28,294. In 1728, Souja Khan formed a corrected Rent Roll, hy which the Provineg of Bengal was divided into twenty-five Thtimgms or Zemindaree Trusts: Tipperah and Noacolly were then ineluded in the [htimam of Jellalpoor. From 1728 to 1765, no alteration seems to have been inade, and when, at the latter date, the Honorable Company assumed the powers of the Dewanny, both Tipperah and Noacolly were under the charge of the Naib of Dacca, the capital of Jellalpoor. From 1765 to 1769, the administration of Jellalpoor was entrusted to two native Officers, Rajah Heymut Singh and one Jusserat Khan. ‘From 1769 to 1772, the country was under the charge of Supervisors, Messrs. Kellsal, Harris, and Lambert. The latter was succeeded by Mr. Greuber, with the title of Collector, in which capacity he continue’ to act, untd the Provincial Council was established in 1774, from which date until 1780, the

revenue was collected’ by Naibs, and the general business of the country was trausacted by European Covenanted Assistants. ( 2 ) In 1781, Tipperalt and Noacolly were constituted into a separate revenue division. The first Officer in charge, Mr. Leake. had no magisterial powers, and the state of the District was consequently as bad as it could be; bands of robbers and armed ruffians infested the whole country, and the burning, not only of villazss, but of human beings, in open day-light, are mentioned in the Collectory Records, as cireunstances of constant oecurrence, so far down as the year 1789, From that date, owing to the appointment of cfficient Collectors, Judges, und Magistrates, things began steadily to improve, and, although the liberty of the subject cannot be said to have heen fully secured before the passing of Section XP Act X. of 1854, it must be admitted that general peace and tranquillity has never been materially disturbed since the beginning of the present Century, = * In the vear 1821, Tipperah was reduced to its present southern limits by the separation of Noacolly the size of which, owing to extensive alluvion, had greatly increased. To describe the gradual consolida- tion of the district by the transfer of numerous Pergunnahs from Mymensingh and Dacca, would involve tyr’ entering into details inconsistent with the genera] nature of this Report. Suffice it to say that the present boundaries of its fiscal and magisterial jurisdictions were not definitively laid down before the year 18380. There are of course numerous traditions coynected with this Zillah, but most of them are not deserving of record; I shall, therefore, only mention three which, being of a general nature, may perhaps be thought interesting. The first is explanatory of

the undoubted fact that there are very few resident Hindoo families of the higher castes in the district. 1 shall relate it in the words of my informant, Baboo Brijosoondor Mittro, Deputy Collector of this Division. * All the country situated to the cast of the Brahmapootra and Megna rivers is called Pandobburjit, or ‘avoided by the sons of Pandoo,—the brothers named Joodhistheer, Bheema, Arjoon, Nocool, and Sohodeb, These persons are the principal characters of the great Sanscrit Epic Poem, the Mohabharut, and the eldest was the emperor of Hustinapoor near Delhi. It is traditionally asserted, that the above five brothers, during their travels in the country, came as tar as the left bank of the above-mentioned rivers, when one of them, Bheema, was sent to ascertain the state of the people. No sooner had he crossed the river than he shouted out unbecoming words, on hearing which, his brothers took him back, considering the people on the eastern side to be barbarous. The stigma thus cast upon this part of the country is still regarded by respectable Hindoos as too marked to be ever forgotten.” lL ruditrons, . The second tradition is to the effect that the old name of Tipperah was Jahajnuggur, or “the city of ships.” It is founded on the circumstance that the revenue of this part of India was at one time monopolized by the Mogul Admiralty Department. One [state still bears the name of the Nowara, or Fleet Estate; and the two largest portions of Pergunnah Seraeel are still known by the peasantry as the Estates of the fourteen and the eight ships, 2 denomination which indicates the ancient form of the revenue paid by them to the State. It was with the aid of fleets collected in this part of the country, that Shaista

Khan, nephew of the Empress Noorjahan, conquered Chittagong, which, in commenoration of the success of Moslem Arms, was at that time called Islamabad. The third tradition is to the effect, that, according to the Mohabharut, out of the corpse of Bhogo- vatee, wife of the god Mohadeb, sprung no less than 51 goddesses, who, by some mysterious process, were at once dispersed over the face of the world; one of them Tripovressurce, or the mistress of the three worlds, took up her residence at OQodeepoor, the former capital of Hill Tipperah. At that place, a large temple has been erected in her honor, which ranks as the second Tirth, or holy shrine, of this part of Bengal. ‘'Fhere can he no doubt that the present name of the District, which at onc time was limitcd to the country situated in the neighbourhood of the Oodeepoor Temple, was originally derived from the appellation of the goddess aforesaid, and thence gradually extended to the whole Zillah. Geographical Features.—-The bulk of this Zillah constitutes a triangle, the apex of which inter- venes, wedge-like, between the river Megna and Hill Tipperah, and the base of which rests on the District of Noacolly. At the South-western corner of the triangle, a long and somewhat narrow strip of land intrudes into the Noacolly District, with which it Shape of Dratrict. ( 3 ) ought. undoubtedly, to be included. As the said tract already forms a separate police division (viz. ‘Thannah Toopkeebugra), such an arrangement would be very practicable, and, by rendering them more compact, would greatly improve both the fiscal and the magisterial jurisdictions. The jurisdiction of the Tipperah Authorities also extends over two tracts of country which are

entirely separated from the main body of the District. One is situated in the heart of the Tipperah Hills, and is bounded by Noacolly to the South. The other skirts the Tipperah Hills, and is bounded by Sylhet to the West. Hach of these tracts, v?z., Montola and Chagulnia (the latter a police divigion), might, with advantage, be included in the jurisdiction of the Districts to which they are adjacent. Outlying portions, The District of Tipperah is bounded, to the North, by the Districts of Mymensingh and Sylhet, and, to the South, by the District of N oacolly. The river Megna forms a natural boundary to the West, and to the East is that portion of Tipperah Proper which has not yet been brought under the Queen’s jurisdiction. The Eastern boundary is, therefore, not merel® a district boundary line but an imperial frontier, a detailed account of which I have tfought it advisable to insert in the Appendix.—( Vide Note 1.) The second staple of this District is the betel-nut. This slender and graceful palm attains the height of about 30 feet, and is in a few Pergunnalis grown to the almost total exclusion of rice. It is raised from seed, 16 planted very close, reaches maturity after about ten years, and, during the succecding fifteen years, gives an average out-turn of about 300 nuts per tree. These nuta were at one time sold at ten and twelve rupees a maund, but although the market price is now only 4 to 6 rupees a maund, a high profit is still derived from their sale. Ketelenut Tree. There can be*no doubt that betel-nut cultivation is, under certain conditions, most unhealthy. This circumstance has been crroncously attributed to some deleterious quality peculiar to the tree itself. But the admitted unhealthiness of those portions of the District where betel-nut is largely grown, can be explained much more casily. The cultivators of this plant usually own a large piece of ground, slightly raised above the level of the country, and surrounded by ditches. In the centre of this land, they build their dwelling houses, und all around them plant betel-nut trees, so thickly, that, as reported by Deputy Collector Bahoo Briyosoondor Mittro, “even at mid-day, sun light does not reach them, free ventilation is altogether stopped, and the air is poisoned by the malarious gases generated from the decomposed vegetable matter with which the surrounding ditches are well nigh tilled.” Under such circumstances, disense in an epidemic form could have been predicted by any person acquainted with the commonest principles of hygienics. Nor would the prediction have proved false; thousands and thousands of the inhabitants of the betel-nut

Pergunnahs have been swept away by cholera and malarious fever of a very virulent kind. A few well-devised sanitary provisionst would at once check the baneful effects, without. materially diminishing the profits of this remunerative branch of agricultural industry. Inhabitants.—The District contains about 7,00,500 inhabitants, or an average of 264 persons per square mile, being 34 more than that of Devonshire, which resembles it precisely in size. The Northern and Eastern portion is more highly populated than the South-eastern, containing the Pergunnahs of Goonanundee, Poorchondee, Doorlace, Mohabutpoor. The non-agricultural element, consisting principally of Llindoos, is very small as compared with the avricultural. Population. The Mahommedans constitute about two-thirds, and the Iindoos one-third of the population. There is very little doubt that the bulk of the former were originally Llindugs, and the process of conversion still continues. The converts usually belong to the lowest Hindoo castes, and are induced to abandon their religion by the reflection, that it is batter to have no caste at all than to belong to a despised one. The same process of reasoning would, undoubtedly, induce them to become Glitistinns, hut, in the first place, the Mahommedan Missionary shee are more

numerous; in the second place, it is the nature of man to follow the example of the createst numer instead of that of an infinitesimal minority. In the third place, the avowed bigotry of ignorant Mahomme- danism is more attractive to uneducated men than the enlightened, because more tolerant, principles of Christianity. Religion. The first, second, and third castes of priests perform religious offices for the higher and middle classes of the Hindoo community. The fourth caste, whose ancestors are said to have disgraced themselves bv receiving pay for the performance of ancestral obsequies, are the priests of the lower castes, with the exception of the Joogees, or weavers, who have priests of the same class as themselves, and the Carpenters (Sootars) who employ in that capacity persons of the Acharjo or Astrologer caste. The Mahommedans of this District have, of course, no caste in the strict sense of the word, but the lower classes are imbued with a great number of Hindoo prejudices, undoubted] -remnants of their former faith. Middle & lower Hindoo Castes. Banos, Mendieants abound in this District. They are called Sanyasees when they take upon themselves vows of celibacy, and Boiragees, when they do not. There are also many female mendicants, called Boishtomees. All these classes are a pest to society ; the male mendicants are the principal perpetrators of larcenies and other petty villainies; the females are just as bad in that respect, and ave women of a notoriously loose character. Mendicanta. Tt would be difficult to find an English equivalent for the so-called Mohunts. These péetsons are dedicated from an early age to celibacy and other austerities, and are usuallv resident in, or near, certain Hindoo temples. They differ from the mendicants nbove-mentioned, in so far as’ the former belong to every caste, whilst the latter must always be of the Brahmin or priestly classes. Another peculiarity is that, as they look on their occupation in the light of a

hereditary office, they always make a point of appointing a successor before their death, usually a poor aud friendless Brahmin boy, who is thus doomed from childhood to a life of misery and of gloomy asceticism. I have in- serted in Note 4, (vide Appendix), a short account of these people. The language of the inhabitants is a mongre] Bengalee, the chief peculiarity of which is that it is very ungrammatical. H is often substituted for initial sand ch, and omitted aftér g, , d, and at the beginning of a word ; 7 is also dropped when followed by a consonant. The Bengalee used in Government Offices may be described in a few words. It is a very imperfect language, quite unfit to express ideas of a complex character. Its Syntax also is rendered so unwieldy by the use of clumsy ger unds, supines, and participles, that it is impossible to be brief without being unidiomatic, or to be idiomatic without being prolix. It is much to be desired that it may soon altogether cease to be used as a medium for official communications or as a language of legal record.

The first quality I attribute, not to any special preference for falsehood, but to the great temptations arising from the manner in which their every-day business is transacted. <All native systems, whether of land measure- ments, of accounts, of rent agreements are, as a rule, remarkable for their want of clearness and practical accuracy, and afford numerous loopholes for deception. Their real nature is veiled by a voluminousness of detail and specious minuteness, which often commands the admiration of a superficial observer, but a careful examination always reveals some Yadieal defect which vitiates the whole. It is under such cireum- stances very natural that the character of the Natives of this District should have been warped by the tortuous nature of the would-be business processes in which they are constantly engaged, and that they should try to avail themselves of the numerous opportunities of fraud which present themselves at every

turn. It appears to me that they could not do otherwise; that long habit has made deceit their second nature; and that there is no probability of their abandoning such sinuous courses until the introduction of sounder methods of business. The second bad quality, that of litigiousness, I attribute to two causes. The first is the ample leisure which the inhabitants of this part of Lower Bengal enjoy; during the greater” part of the year, they have absolutely nothing to do, and, as they much affect the unhealthy pleasure derivable from litiga- tion, they resort to Courts in phedisnee to the same promptings which induce idle and uneduented Europeans to frequent taverns and othét dangerous haunts. If the cause were removed, the evil would nlso disappear; if the Natives of this District were furnished with better means of communication, and, therefore, with more numerous opportunities of driving lucrative and engrossing trades, they would ceax tv institute cases, as they do now, from sheer love of excitement. A second cause of litigiousness is the unsettled nature of the rights of landlords. As tenants and landlords constitute the bulk of the population, the desire of the former to contest, and of the latter to enforce, dubious privileges and claims, both necessitates and perpetuates litigation. THE limits of the Queen’s and Tipperah Rajah’s jurisdiction were, for a long time, the source of constant disputes, until, in the year 1852, they were finally adjusted and mapped by Measrs. Leicester and Campbell, apecially

appointed for that purpose. Unfortunately, those gentlemen did not erect any boundary marks. Great difficulty was, therefore, experienced by the Survey Department in executing their award. On visiting the spot, it was found that, in many cases, the lines mapped by them ran over hill and dale, and through large blocks of jungle, with the most ruthless disregard of expediency. Masonry pillars and telegraph posts are now being erected at all the angles of the boundary, which, when completed, will clearly define its general outline. Tt will, however, be necessary, in many places, to erect additional land marks. The spots on which the present pillars and posts are erected, are, often, so far apart, and the nature of the intervening country is such, that it is impag- sible to sce more than one at a time. It is, therefore, clear that, in such-localities, the boundary will not be practically defined, and that disputes between cultivators will be frequent and by no means ensy to decide. The best and cheapest method of erccting such additional marks would be to offer a certain sum (half of which shoyld be defrayed by the Rajah), for the construction of large mounds (say seven feet hich), where the pillars and posts do not sufficiently define the boundary; such aum to be paid to the inhabitants of the frontier villages. Five rupees a mound would, I think, be amply sufficient for the purpose. A term of one year might be allowed and the price. paid, only after ascertaining that the mounds had been properly made, and at such distances apart as to render it possible for any person standing, at any point between any two mounds, to see both with ease.

The Tipperahs, or inhabitants of the Tipperah Till Rangers, are said by some to be colonists from Moneepoorgf, from which place they were driven by 2 Burmese invasion. But there can be little doubt that the opinion of those, who nasert them to have inhabited this part of the country from time immemorial, is equally well-founded. Nothing is known about the ancient history of these people, but tradition names as their first king Asango, who is said to be the ancestor of Trilochun, mentioned, in the Mahabhurut} as the Rajah of Tipperah. The religion, now prevailing, is a forin of Hindoo idolatry, but it is said that, before the accession of Trilochun, they worshipped no idols, but objects of nature, e. g. trees, stones, animals. A trace of their old faith is to be found in their present practice of sticking a bamboo in the ground, during one of their religious festivals, and worshipping 1t. The language of these bill men is very rude and primitive, but I cannot yet say to what class it belongs. Pundit Jugdish Surma, the head master of the Normal Vernacular School, has prepared, under my direction, a Tipperah vocabulary aud grammar, which will duly forwarded to the Asiatic Society. ( 39 ) I have, therefore, no doubt that philological scholars will soon be able to assign to the Tipperah dialect its due place in the great family of languages. The tribes of the Tipperahs are four in number: the Rajbunsoes, Nowatyahs, Jomatecas, Reyangas. The

first is looked upon as highly respectable, whilst the last is held in very Jow estimation. The Tipperah villages, or rather hamlets, are called Barces. They are under the control of Chowdrees, whose orders are implicitly obeyed, whose office is hereditary, and who decide all small disputes. The priests of the first three tribes are called Tojaces, but the Reyangas have pricsts of their own; celibacy is not practised by them. — | : No religious ceremony is necessary for a marriage, but only the consent of the parents, If the bridegroom can give a dower, the marriage takes place at once, but, if he cannot, he must serve one year in his father-in-law’s house. Early marriages are not prevalent, and polygamy, though not objected to, is very rare. Ig prostitutes take an oath to behave well in future, they can marry without difficulty. Tipperahs eat flesh of every description except beef; they burn their dead, and after the decease of a relation, abstain from meat for a week. Both men and women are fond of drinking and dancing. They are, asa rule, truthful and simple-minded, No man is looked upon as a person of any importance until he is married, when he has to pay g tax for his family as a whole. ; Their method of agriculture is very peculiar, and is generally known by the namo of Jhoom cultivation (derived from a Tipperah word meaning “to burn”). In the months of February and March, they cut down the Hill bamboo. Atihe beginning of the rains, they. mix seeds of paddy and cotton in a wicker basket, and finally sow them along with turmeric, pepper, ginger, millet, kutchoo, and oil seeds, in small holes, which they dig with an iron instrument called

a tookooree, resembling the common Bengalee kodalee. Tach plant ripens at its proper season, e. y., the paddy about the 15th of July and in September according to the species to which it belongs; and the cotton from 15th October to 15th December. The success of the latter crop depends on the ahsence of heavy rains from 15th October to 15th November. If the rains are very heavy, most of the pods rot and fall off, and those which remain produce a very inferior kind of eotton.
